645.title: Only one arrow
645.hook: the untaught feel pain and then a second arrow of distress (SN 36.6)
645.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the arrow simile in teaching about pain and illness, and some modern mindfulness programs for chronic pain draw on the distinction between physical pain and the distress added to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the nun Vajira and your line, a chariot of parts. Did you take a big word apart? Today, a teaching from year one, the second arrow, but read whole, with the part people usually skip. Day six hundred forty-five.

You stub your toe on the bed frame at six in the morning. That's the pain. Then, within half a second: who put this bed here, why does this always happen to me, this whole day is ruined. And then, if you're like a lot of people, you reach for something to make it go away, your phone, a snack, an hour of a show. Three moves, one tiny injury. The second arrow is a teaching many people know. But the discourse it comes from keeps going past the second arrow, to that third move. Today: only one arrow.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE AT SIX A.M.` → `THIS ALWAYS HAPPENS TO ME.` → `THEN, REACHING FOR THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: SN 36.6 is called the Arrow. The Buddha asks the monks: the untaught person feels pleasant, painful and neutral feelings. So does the well-taught disciple. What's the difference? Then the picture. When an untaught person is touched by a painful feeling, they sorrow, grieve, lament, beat their chest, and become distraught. So they feel two feelings, one in the body and one in the mind. It's as if a man were struck by an arrow, and then a second arrow hit him in the same place. Here's the part that's often skipped. Being touched by pain, the text says, the untaught person seeks delight in sensual pleasure. Why? Because, the Buddha says, they know no other way out of painful feeling except sensual pleasure. So pain leads to resistance, and resistance leads to reaching for pleasure, and the pleasure feeds a habit of wanting. The discourse names three underlying tendencies stirred up along the way: toward aversion, toward lust, and toward not seeing clearly. A whole cycle, from one stubbed toe. The well-taught disciple, touched by the same pain, doesn't sorrow, lament or become distraught. They feel one feeling, the bodily one, not the mental one. One arrow. And because they know another way out of pain than pleasure, they don't need to reach. Notice what the text doesn't promise. The first arrow still lands, even on the well-taught. The body still hurts. What changes is everything that usually comes after.
screen: `THE SAME FEELINGS, A DIFFERENT RESPONSE` · `A SECOND ARROW IN THE SAME PLACE` · `NO OTHER WAY OUT BUT PLEASURE` · `THE FIRST ARROW STILL LANDS` · then, large: `ONLY ONE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find one small discomfort in the body right now. A tight back, a sore spot, a restless leg. Feel it as plainly as you can: where it is, its size, whether it pulses or stays. That's the first arrow. Now watch for the second: a thought like I hate this, or this is going to ruin my day. If it comes, notice it, and come back to just the sensation. And watch for the third: the urge to fix it with something nice. Let the urge be there without following it. One arrow. The bell holds the time.
Only one arrow. In SN 36.6, the well-taught feel the pain of the body without the second arrow of distress, and without reaching for pleasure as the only way out. Today's word.
Your line: only one arrow. The next time something stings today, feel it, and then catch the second arrow, or the reach for comfort, before it lands. Day six hundred forty-five.

myth: the well-taught disciple stops feeling bodily pain
the first arrow still lands; what drops away is the second.
SN 36.6 says the untaught reach for pleasure to escape pain
because they know no other way out of painful feeling.

toward aversion, toward lust, and toward not seeing clearly.

fork.setup: a painful feeling has just hit you. according to SN 36.6, what does the untaught person do next?
options: grieve and lament, then reach for sensual pleasure.
feel it plainly and let it pass.
fork.reveal: the untaught add a second arrow of distress, then look for pleasure, because they know no other escape.

original.note: Pali salla: an arrow or dart. SN 36.6 is the Sallatha Sutta, the arrow.

trapdoor: what you thought: only one arrow means toughing out the pain.
what it means: in SN 36.6, feeling the bodily pain without adding mental distress, and without reaching for pleasure as the only escape.

what a scholar hears: SN 36 is the Vedana Samyutta, the chapter on feeling; the sutta ties each kind of feeling to an underlying tendency, anusaya: aversion with pain, lust with pleasure, ignorance with the neutral.

646.title: Foam on the river
646.hook: form like foam, feeling like bubbles, perception a mirage, formations a hollow stalk, consciousness a magic show (SN 22.95)
646.howItsDone: Many Buddhists contemplate the five aggregates through images like these, and teachers in many traditions use the foam, the bubble and the mirage to teach impermanence.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the arrow, read whole, and your line, only one arrow. Did you catch the reach for comfort? Today the Buddha sits by the Ganges and points at the water. Day six hundred forty-six.

The Buddha is staying at Ayojjha, on the bank of the Ganges. The river is wide and brown and moving, and it's carrying a big lump of foam downstream, the kind that gathers where water churns. He tells the monks: suppose someone with good eyes looked closely at that foam. Examined it carefully. What would they find? They'd find it empty, hollow, without anything solid inside. Then, one after another, he points at four more things you could see on a riverbank or at a fair. Five pictures. Today: foam on the river.
screen: `ON THE BANK OF THE GANGES.` → `A LUMP OF FOAM, FLOATING BY.` → `LOOK CLOSELY: WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: SN 22.95 matches each of the five heaps, the parts of a person we met with Vajira's chariot, to something you can see. Form, the body, is like that lump of foam. Feeling is like a bubble. The Buddha sets the scene: in autumn, when it rains in big drops, a bubble rises on the water and bursts. Pleasant, painful, neither: up and gone. Perception, the mind's labeling, is like a mirage in the last month of the hot season, shimmering on the road, convincing, not there. Formations, our habits and intentions, are like a banana tree. A man goes looking for heartwood with a sharp axe. He cuts down a big, straight, young plantain trunk, and peels it, layer after layer, and finds no heartwood at all. Not even softwood. Just layers. And consciousness is like a magic show, a trick put on by a conjurer at a crossroads. Someone with good eyes sees through it. Each picture is chosen carefully. Foam has a shape, but you can't build with it. Bubbles last a moment. A mirage misleads honestly, it really looks like water. The plantain is layers all the way down. The magic show is the most striking: it doesn't say consciousness isn't happening, it says it isn't what it appears to be. The point isn't gloom. The Buddha says that one who sees this way grows disenchanted, and through dispassion is freed. The verse at the end adds a gentle note: this body, when life, heat and consciousness leave it, lies cast aside, food for others. Foam, after all, is still beautiful on a river. You just don't try to hold it.
screen: `FORM: A LUMP OF FOAM` · `FEELING: A RAINDROP BUBBLE` · `PERCEPTION: A MIRAGE, FORMATIONS: A PLANTAIN` · `CONSCIOUSNESS: A MAGIC SHOW` · then, large: `FOAM ON THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at foam or bubbles right now: the top of a glass of something fizzy, soap in the sink, a puddle in the rain. If not, picture one clearly. Watch a bubble form, sit, and burst. Then turn to your own feelings as they come, the small pleasant ones, the small unpleasant ones. See each rise and burst, like the raindrops on the river. No need to push any away. Just watch them go. The bell holds the time.
Foam on the river. In SN 22.95, form is foam, feeling a bubble, perception a mirage, formations a plantain trunk, consciousness a magic show. Today's word.
Your line: foam on the river. When a feeling grips you today, picture it as a bubble rising on rainwater, and watch it burst. Day six hundred forty-six.

pairs: a mirage in the hot season

fork.reveal: just layers, not even softwood: the Buddha's picture of formations, habits and intentions with no solid core.

original.note: Pali phena: foam. SN 22.95 is the Phenapindupama Sutta, the simile of the lump of foam.

trapdoor: what you thought: foam on the river is just a pretty image.
what it means: in SN 22.95, five pictures for the five heaps: foam, bubble, mirage, plantain trunk and magic show, none with a solid core.

what a scholar hears: the foam, bubble and mirage images reappear in later Buddhist literature, including the Dhammapada's verse comparing the world to a bubble and a mirage, and the Mahayana's Diamond Sutra.

647.title: The burden
647.hook: the five heaps are the burden; craving is the one who picks it up (SN 22.22)
647.howItsDone: The Bhara Sutta is studied in many Buddhist traditions, and its closing verse is sometimes recited or chanted as a reminder that laying down craving brings ease.

segments.voice: Yesterday: five pictures by the Ganges, and your line, foam on the river. Did a feeling burst like a bubble? Today the same five heaps, but this time as something heavy on your back. Day six hundred forty-seven.

Watch someone come home after a long day. The bag drops off one shoulder onto the floor, the shoes come off, and there's a sound, half sigh, half laugh. The body knows the relief of setting something down before the mind has said a word. Most of us carry more than a bag, though, and we don't notice how heavy it is until the moment it's off. The Buddha gave a very short teaching at Savatthi built on exactly that moment: what's heavy, who carries it, how it gets picked up, and what it's like to put it down. Today: the burden.
screen: `THE BAG HITS THE FLOOR.` → `HALF SIGH, HALF LAUGH.` → `WHAT ARE YOU CARRYING?`

segments.voice: SN 22.22 has four parts, like a riddle with its answers. What is the burden? The five heaps that are clung to: body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. Not the heaps themselves, notice, but the heaps as grasped, taken as me and mine. Who carries the burden? The person, the Buddha says, this venerable one of such a name and such a family. You, by name. What is taking up the burden? Craving: the thirst that leads to more becoming, delighting here and there, craving for pleasure, for existence, for nonexistence. And what is laying the burden down? The complete fading away and ending of that same craving, letting it go, being free of it. Then a short verse. The five heaps are burdens indeed, and the person carries them. Picking up the burden is suffering in the world. Putting it down is happiness. So the burden is real, and somebody is carrying it, and the picking up happens through craving. Which means the putting down happens there too. Not by throwing away the body or the mind, but by loosening the grip that keeps lifting them. One historical footnote: an early Buddhist school, the Personalists, pointed to this sutta to argue that the person is real in some sense, since someone carries the burden. Other schools replied that the person here is a conventional name, like the chariot. The debate ran for centuries, and Buddhist schools still read the passage differently. What they share is the last line: putting it down is happiness.
screen: `THE BURDEN: THE HEAPS, CLUNG TO` · `THE CARRIER: THIS PERSON, BY NAME` · `PICKING IT UP: CRAVING` · `PUTTING IT DOWN: CRAVING ENDS` · then, large: `PUT IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice one thing you're carrying right now. Not a bag: a worry, a resentment, a job you've decided only you can do. Feel where it sits in the body, shoulders, chest, jaw. Ask quietly: what keeps picking this up? Usually it's a wanting: to be right, to be safe, to be in control. Now, just for these two minutes, let it rest on the floor beside you. You can pick it up again after. For now, feel the shoulders drop. The bell holds the time.
The burden. In SN 22.22, the five heaps clung to are the burden, the person carries it, craving picks it up, and its ending puts it down. Today's word.
Your line: put it down. Set down one burden today, even for an hour: a grudge, a task you can hand off, a worry you've checked three times. Day six hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 647 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOG ON A LEASH.`

the carrier is the person; craving is the taking up of the burden.

fork.reveal: craving is what picks the burden up, so its fading away is what lays it down. putting it down, the verse says, is happiness.

original.note: Pali bhara: a burden or load. SN 22.22 is the Bhara Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: the burden means your responsibilities.
what it means: in SN 22.22, the five heaps clung to; the person carries them, craving picks them up, and craving's ending lays them down.

what a scholar hears: the Pudgalavada, or Personalist, schools cited the Bhara Sutta for a person neither the same as nor different from the heaps; other schools, including the Theravada, rejected that reading.

648.title: The dog on a leash
648.hook: a dog tied to a post circles it endlessly: clinging to self (SN 22.99)
648.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use the leash simile to explain identity view, the twenty ways of taking the five aggregates as self, which many traditions treat as the first fetter to be broken.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the burden, and your line, put it down. What did you set down, even for an hour? Today the heaps again, and an animal you've probably seen outside a shop. Day six hundred forty-eight.

Outside a grocery store, a dog is tied to a post. Its person went in five minutes ago. The dog walks one way around the post, then the other way, then back, wrapping and unwrapping its leash, sitting, standing, circling again. It's going somewhere and nowhere at the same time. Everyone who walks past smiles at it, because it's so clearly waiting for something it can't make happen faster. The Buddha used that very picture, a dog tied to a stake, and he wasn't talking about dogs. Today: the dog on a leash.
screen: `TIED OUTSIDE THE STORE.` → `ONE WAY AROUND, THEN THE OTHER.` → `GOING NOWHERE, FAST.`

segments.voice: SN 22.99 begins with a large claim. This round of wandering, the Buddha says, has no beginning that can be found. Beings roam on and on, blocked by not knowing, tied by craving. A time may come, he says, when the great ocean dries up, when this great earth is burned up. Even so, the suffering of beings who wander like this doesn't end. Then the picture. Suppose a dog on a leash is tied to a strong post or pillar. It just runs and circles around that post. In the same way, the untaught person regards the body as self, or self as having a body, or the body as inside the self, or the self as inside the body. The same with feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. And so they run and circle around those five, and aren't freed from them. The post is the heaps. The leash is taking them as me. The dog isn't evil and isn't stupid. It's just tied. And every lap it runs, it's doing something real, moving, trying, hoping. It's simply the case that the circle is set by the post. Notice the four ways of taking the body as self. They're precise. Some people think, I am my body. Some think, I have a body. Some think, my body is in me. Some, I am in my body. The sutta says these are all ways of being tied. The good news is in the same picture. A dog that isn't tied doesn't circle. The text, here and in the next discourse, goes on: one who doesn't take the heaps as self isn't bound to the post.
screen: `NO BEGINNING CAN BE FOUND` · `A DOG TIED TO A STRONG POST` · `THE POST IS THE HEAPS, THE LEASH IS ME` · `UNTIED, THE DOG DOESN'T CIRCLE` · then, large: `ROUND AND ROUND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice one thought you keep circling. A worry about money. Something someone said. How you look. Watch it come around again, the way the dog comes round the post. Then look for the post: what's it tied to? Often it's a sense of me: my reputation, my body, my plans. You don't have to cut the leash today. Just see it. Seeing the post is already a little slack in the leash. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The dog on a leash. In SN 22.99, the untaught person circles the five heaps like a dog tied to a post, because they take them as self. Today's word.
screen: `THE DOG ON A LEASH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: round and round. When you catch yourself on the same lap of a thought today, ask once: what post am I tied to? Day six hundred forty-eight.

myth: SN 22.99 says the ocean drying up would end beings' suffering
even when the ocean dries up and the earth burns, it says suffering doesn't end for those still wandering.
the sutta lists four ways of taking the body as self
body as self, self with a body, body in self, self in body.
the dog in the simile is called foolish
it isn't blamed; it's tied, and the circle is set by the post.

fork.setup: you're the dog, tied to a post, running in circles. by SN 22.99, what would let you stop?
options: not be tied: not take the heaps as self.
fork.reveal: the circle comes from the leash. the texts say one who doesn't take the heaps as self isn't bound to the post.

original.note: Pali gaddula: a leash or strap. SN 22.99 is the Gaddulabaddha Sutta, the one bound by a leash.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dog on a leash is about being stuck in a routine.
what it means: in SN 22.99, circling the five heaps because we take them as self.
what a scholar hears: the four ways per heap, times five heaps, give the twenty forms of identity view, sakkaya-ditthi, which the texts list as the first of the fetters broken at stream-entry.

649.title: More than the oceans
649.hook: the tears shed over countless lives are more than the four oceans (SN 15.3)
649.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions mark grief with chanting, merit-making and memorial rites for the dead, and teachings like the tears and the oceans are sometimes shared at funerals and in times of loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dog circling its post, and your line, round and round. Did you find your post? Today the Buddha asks the monks a question about water, and the answer is tears. Day six hundred forty-nine.

Most people can remember the worst cry of their life. Where they were sitting. What the light looked like. The way it came in waves, and how tired the body felt after. Maybe it was a death, or a breakup, or a phone call. Grief has a way of making each loss feel like the only one in the world. In a short chapter of the Connected Sayings about the long round of lives, the Buddha takes that one private cry and sets it beside a very large body of water. Today: more than the oceans.
screen: `THE WORST CRY OF YOUR LIFE.` → `IT COMES IN WAVES.` → `BESIDE A VERY LARGE WATER.`

segments.voice: SN 15.3 is a question and answer. The Buddha asks the monks: which is more? The tears you have shed while wandering this long round, weeping and wailing because you were joined with what you disliked and parted from what you loved, or the water in the four great oceans? The monks answer straight from what they've been taught. The tears, sir. The tears are more. Yes, the Buddha says. And then he names them, one by one. For a long time you have suffered the death of a mother. The tears shed over that alone are more than the four oceans. The death of a father. A brother. A sister. A son. A daughter. The loss of relatives, of wealth, the suffering of illness. Each time, the same refrain: more than the water in the four great oceans. It's a hard teaching to sit with, and the text doesn't soften it. But notice its tone. It isn't scolding anyone for crying. It's almost tender: you've lost so much, for so long. It takes grief seriously enough to measure it against the sea. Then it draws a conclusion: enough. This is reason enough to grow weary of the round, to let the craving that keeps it turning fade, and to be free. Buddhists hold the idea of many lives in different ways. Many take rebirth quite literally; some modern teachers read it more as moment to moment. Either way, the picture of the tears holds something true: no grief is the first, and no one grieves alone.
screen: `TEARS, OR THE FOUR OCEANS?` · `A MOTHER, A FATHER, A CHILD` · `IT TAKES GRIEF SERIOUSLY` · `REASON ENOUGH TO BE FREE` · then, large: `MORE THAN THE OCEANS.`

segments.voice: Sit gently. If it feels right, let one old grief come to mind. Not the rawest one, if that's too much. Something you've lived with a while. Don't push it away and don't dig into it. Just let it be here, the way you'd let an old friend sit beside you. Breathe with it. Then widen the picture a little: so many people, across so much time, have felt exactly this. Let that be company, not a burden. If it's too heavy, come back to the breath at any time. The bell holds the time.
More than the oceans. In SN 15.3, the tears shed over loss across the long round are more than the water in the four great oceans. Today's word.
Your line: more than the oceans. If someone near you is grieving today, remember the oceans, and be gentle. If it's you, be gentle with yourself. Day six hundred forty-nine.

pairs: joined with the disliked, parted from the loved

myth: the Buddha scolds the monks for crying
the tone is almost tender: it measures grief against the sea and takes it seriously.
the sutta names the deaths of mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, sons and daughters
each with the same refrain: more than the four great oceans.

fork.setup: the Buddha asks you: which is more, the tears you've shed over the long round, or the water in the four great oceans? what do you answer?
fork.reveal: the monks answer the tears, and the Buddha agrees, naming each kind of loss in turn.

original.note: Pali assu: a tear. SN 15.3 is the Assu Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: more than the oceans is a poetic way to say very sad.
what it means: in SN 15.3, the tears shed over losses across countless lives outweigh the water in the four great oceans.
what a scholar hears: SN 15 is the Anamatagga Samyutta, the chapter on the round without discoverable beginning; its similes measure time and loss in oceans, mountains and heaps of bones.

650.title: No beginning to find
650.hook: count your mothers with twigs, your fathers with balls of clay, and the earth runs out first (SN 15.1–2)
650.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism especially, students practice recognizing all beings as having once been their mothers, as a basis for compassion; teachers in other traditions draw on the same chapter of the Samyutta Nikaya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tears and the four oceans, and your line, more than the oceans. Were you gentle with someone's grief? Today the same chapter opens, with grass and clay and a counting game no one can finish. Day six hundred fifty.

Family trees are popular. You can send off a sample of your spit and get back a map of where your great-great-grandparents lived. Go back far enough, though, and the branches multiply faster than anyone can count. Two parents, four grandparents, eight, sixteen, and soon the chart is wider than the page. The Buddha starts the chapter on the long round of lives with a family tree too. But instead of paper, he uses all the grass in India, and then the whole earth. Today: no beginning to find.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE BY MAIL.` → `TWO, FOUR, EIGHT, SIXTEEN.` → `NOW USE ALL THE GRASS.`

segments.voice: SN 15.1 opens the chapter with a sentence the next twenty discourses keep returning to. This round of wandering, monks, is without a discoverable beginning. No first point can be found where beings, blocked by not knowing and tied by craving, started roaming. Then the picture. Suppose someone cut all the grass, sticks, branches and leaves in all of India, gathered them in one heap, and cut them into little sticks, each four fingers long. Then, laying them down one at a time, they counted: this is my mother, this is my mother's mother, and on and on. The grass and sticks of India would run out before the line of mothers did. SN 15.2 does the same with the earth. Roll the whole earth into balls of clay the size of a jujube seed, and put them down: this is my father, this is my father's father. The earth runs out first. Then the same conclusion: for so long you have experienced loss and suffering. It's enough to grow weary of all this, and to be free. The images are meant to stretch the mind until it gives up trying to find the edge. Not a large number, just none at all: no beginning to find. A little later in the same chapter, the Buddha draws out one surprising consequence. It is hard, he says, to find a being who has not at some time been your mother, or your father, your brother, sister, son or daughter. Many Buddhist teachers have built a whole practice of kindness on that line: everyone you meet may once have been family.
screen: `WITHOUT A DISCOVERABLE BEGINNING` · `GRASS AND STICKS: MY MOTHER'S MOTHER` · `BALLS OF CLAY: MY FATHER'S FATHER` · `EVERYONE MAY ONCE HAVE BEEN FAMILY` · then, large: `NO BEGINNING TO FIND.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone you'll see today who isn't family. A coworker, a cashier, a neighbor, someone you find difficult. Picture them clearly. Then, gently, try the old thought: at some time, in some way, this one may have been my mother, my father, my brother or sister. You don't have to believe it as a fact to let it change how they look. Notice any softening. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
No beginning to find. In SN 15.1 and 15.2, the grass of India and the clay of the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers does: the round has no discoverable beginning. Today's word.
Your line: no beginning to find. Treat one person today as you would family, with a little more patience than they'd expect. Day six hundred fifty.

pairs: balls of clay from the earth

it gives no number at all: no beginning can be found.
the line of mothers outlasts all the grass of India
the grass and sticks run out first, the sutta says.
the chapter says it's hard to find a being who hasn't been your mother

fork.setup: you're cutting all the grass of India into little sticks, one for each mother back through your line. what happens?
options: the line of mothers and the grass end together.
fork.reveal: the grass runs out, and the line of mothers goes on: the round has no beginning to find.

original.note: Pali anamatagga: without a discoverable beginning. SN 15 is the Anamatagga Samyutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: no beginning to find means the past is long.
what it means: in SN 15.1–2, the round of lives has no discoverable beginning; the grass and the earth run out before the line of mothers and fathers.

what a scholar hears: anamatagga is usually explained as 'whose first point is not known'; the same chapter's line that all beings have been our mothers became the root of Tibetan practices for developing compassion.

651.title: The whole of it
651.hook: Ananda says good friendship is half the holy life; no, the whole (SN 45.2)
651.howItsDone: Buddhist communities in every tradition practice together in sanghas, temples and retreat groups, and many teachers name spiritual friendship as central to practice, citing this sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grass, clay and the line of mothers, and your line, no beginning to find. Who did you treat as family? Today Ananda makes a guess about friendship, and closes our week by being corrected. Day six hundred fifty-one.

Think of the friend who got you to the gym when you didn't want to go. The one who told you, kindly, that the relationship wasn't good for you. The one who just showed up, again and again, until you were the kind of person who shows up too. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, had been thinking about friends like that. He comes to the Buddha in a small Sakyan town and says, with some confidence, that he's worked out how much good friends are worth. He's about to be told he's off by half. Today: the whole of it.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO GOT YOU THERE.` → `ANANDA HAS A THEORY.` → `OFF BY HALF.`

segments.voice: SN 45.2 is short and has a surprise in the middle. Ananda says: half of the holy life, venerable sir, is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. A generous estimate. The Buddha's reply is immediate. Not so, Ananda, not so. Good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship is the entire holy life. Then he explains. When someone has a good friend, you can expect them to develop the noble eightfold path. Right view, right intention, all the way through. A good friend doesn't just help with the path. They're how the path gets walked. Then he points to himself. It's by relying on me as a good friend, the Buddha says, that beings subject to birth are freed from birth, beings subject to aging, from aging, subject to sorrow, from sorrow. The teacher calls himself a friend. The Pali phrase is kalyanamittata, having a lovely friend, a good friend. Kalyana means beautiful, good, and mitta means friend. It doesn't mean someone who agrees with everything. In the texts, a good friend speaks honestly, can bear to be told things, and points you toward what helps. Look back at this week. One arrow instead of two. Foam on the river. The burden, and putting it down. A dog circling its post. Tears more than the oceans. A line of mothers with no beginning. Heavy material, most of it. And the week ends here, with the Buddha saying that the way through all of it is walked with friends.
